title: Hierocles' circles
hookLine: picture circles of care, self, family, town, humanity, and draw them inward (Hierocles, in Stobaeus)

lines: THEN A FACE, A FAMILY, A FRIEND.
cards: Watch a baby for an afternoon. First she cares about herself: warm, fed, held. Soon she knows her mother's face from every other face.
Then her dad, a sibling, the dog. Later, a best friend; later still, a whole school she'll cheer for at a game. Care grows outward in rings, like a stone dropped in a pond.
The Stoics noticed this too, and thought it wasn't only a story about growing up. It was an assignment for adults.

teach.b: Oikeiosis is a hard word to translate.

It comes from oikos, house or home, and means something like making your own, or coming to feel at home with. The Stoics said every living creature starts with oikeiosis toward itself: it cares for its own life.
In humans that care keeps widening, until we feel at home with more and more of the world.
Hierocles, a later Stoic, turned this into a picture, and we know it because a later collector named Stobaeus copied it into his anthology. Imagine yourself surrounded by circles.
The smallest holds your own mind and body. The next, your parents, siblings, partner, children. Then aunts, uncles, cousins.
Then your neighbors, your town, your country. The biggest holds the whole human race. Here's the practical part, and it's charming.
The job, Hierocles says, is to draw the circles inward, pulling each ring a little closer to the center.

His tip: speak of cousins as brothers and sisters, of uncles and aunts as fathers and mothers. Words change how near people feel. You don't pretend a stranger is your child; you just move them in one ring.

Most of what Hierocles wrote was lost, until a papyrus with part of his ethics turned up in Egypt. So this picture survived by two thin threads, an anthology and a scrap of papyrus, and now it's in your ear.

how: Stoic practitioners sometimes picture Hierocles' concentric circles and deliberately treat people in outer circles with the care usually kept for inner ones.

o: care that starts with yourself and widens to all people
an old Greek rule for managing a home's money
loyalty to your own household before anyone else

s: Hierocles wanted people to erase their families
he wanted outer circles drawn closer, not inner ones removed.
part of Hierocles' ethics survived on a papyrus found in Egypt
the circles reached us another way, through Stobaeus.
for the Stoics, oikeiosis starts with care for oneself
every creature first cares for its own life, then care widens.

games.q: you want to draw your circles in. what does Hierocles suggest about your cousins?
o: speak of them as brothers and sisters.
games.why: he says to call cousins brothers and sisters, and uncles and aunts fathers and mothers: words move people a ring closer.

practice: Picture the circles around you: you at the center, your closest people, your wider family, your street or your coworkers, your town, your country, everyone.
Find one person out in an outer ring, a neighbor you nod to, a coworker you barely know. On each breath in, bring them one ring closer, just one, and notice how it feels to hold them there.

wordCard.voice: Oikeiosis. Greek for making your own, feeling at home with: care that starts with the self and widens to all people.

orig.note: Greek: making one's own, familiarization; from oikos, home.

carryVoice: Your line: draw the circles in. A cousin called a sister is already one ring nearer. Two hundred ninety-one days now.

sources.ref: Hierocles, On Appropriate Acts, in Stobaeus, Anthology 4.27.23
Diogenes Laërtius 7.85 (a creature's first impulse is toward itself)
